Barrett oesophagus with high-grade dysplasia is now treated by endoscopic eradication (EMR of visible lesions plus radiofrequency ablation); oesophagectomy is reserved for failures or invasive disease.
The cervical oesophagus is supplied by the inferior thyroid artery, the thoracic part by aortic branches and the abdominal part by the left gastric artery.
Low-grade dysplasia in Barrett oesophagus: high-dose PPI and repeat endoscopy at 6 months; confirmed persistent LGD is then offered radiofrequency ablation.
New reflux symptoms in a 72-year-old need OGD first, to see the mucosa, take biopsies and exclude malignancy; pH studies come later if the diagnosis is unclear.
Young dyspeptic patients without alarm features are managed by ‘test and treat’: confirm H. pylori (urea breath or stool antigen test) before giving eradication therapy.

Eradication therapy should follow a positive test (urea breath or stool antigen); a 59-year-old with persistent symptoms also needs OGD if they do not settle.
A patient with previous ulcer starting an NSAID should be tested and treated for H. pylori and given PPI gastroprotection.
